label: Robot Control
notes: This chapter asks how feedback laws turn desired motion or desired contact into stable robot action. Across printed pages 403 to 460 we move from joint-space error dynamics through computed torque to force and impedance control, treating every controller as a deliberately chosen error equation rather than a torque recipe.

label: The Control Objective
notes: Motion control demands that the configuration track a reference trajectory, expressed either in joint coordinates or in task space through the Jacobian. We define the error as desired minus actual, and the entire chapter studies how to shape the differential equation that this error obeys.

label: Error Dynamics and Stability
notes: A controller is judged by the differential equation it imposes on the tracking error. If that equation is linear and its characteristic roots sit in the open left half plane, the error decays to zero. Stability is therefore a statement about eigenvalues, not about any single torque value.

label: PID Joint Control
notes: Proportional, integral, and derivative terms act on the joint error directly. The proportional gain pulls toward the target, derivative damps oscillation, and integral erases steady offsets from gravity or friction. Without integral action a constant disturbance leaves a permanent steady-state error.

label: Second-Order Error and Damping
notes: With proportional and derivative feedback the error obeys a mass-spring-damper equation. The damping ratio decides the transient: under-damped responses overshoot and ring, over-damped responses crawl, and critical damping gives the fastest settling without overshoot. Gains are chosen to place that ratio at one.

label: Choosing Gains for Critical Damping
notes: Specifying a natural frequency and a unit damping ratio fixes both gains: the proportional gain equals the natural frequency squared and the derivative gain equals twice the natural frequency. Larger natural frequency means faster response but demands more torque and amplifies any unmodeled dynamics.

label: Feedforward Control
notes: Feedforward injects the torque predicted by the model along the planned trajectory, so feedback only has to correct the residual. When the model is accurate the feedback effort shrinks toward zero, but every modeling error reappears as a tracking error that feedback alone must absorb.

label: Computed-Torque Control
notes: Computed torque uses the mass matrix, Coriolis vector, and gravity to cancel the nonlinear dynamics exactly, leaving a clean linear error equation in every joint. This feedback linearization decouples the joints so that a single pair of gains delivers identical second-order behavior throughout the workspace.

label: Linearized Error Dynamics
notes: After cancellation the commanded acceleration equals the desired acceleration plus a proportional and derivative correction on the error. The closed-loop error then satisfies a decoupled linear system whose decay rate we set directly, which is exactly the second-order shaping seen earlier, now valid globally.

label: Force Control
notes: When the end-effector presses on a stiff environment, position commands become meaningless and we regulate the contact wrench instead. A force controller compares measured to desired wrench and adjusts torque through the Jacobian transpose, often adding damping so the loop stays stable against the environment stiffness.

label: Hybrid Motion-Force Control
notes: A contact task splits Cartesian directions into a motion subspace and an orthogonal force subspace. Selection or projection matrices route position feedback into free directions and force feedback into constrained ones, so the robot slides along a surface while pressing into it with a commanded normal force.

label: Impedance and Admittance Control
notes: Impedance control renders a chosen mass-spring-damper between displacement and contact force, letting the end-effector feel compliant rather than rigid. Admittance is the dual: measured force drives a reference motion. Tuning the virtual stiffness and damping trades tracking accuracy against gentle, stable interaction.

label: Synthesis and Pitfalls
notes: Every controller here is a chosen error dynamics layered on the robot's geometry and dynamics. High gains can mask model error until contact or saturation exposes it, and force control without a contact model is ill posed. Hybrid and impedance laws are projections of task intent onto motion and force.
